# RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter reviews the studies on which the research builds and identifies the gaps that it addresses. It first covers multi-task learning and negative transfer, then multi-task optimizers and their training cost, and then disaster text datasets and the processing of Taglish. It ends with a matrix that compares the key studies and a synthesis of the gaps that the research questions address.

## Multi-Task Learning and Negative Transfer

Multi-task learning trains one model on several related tasks at the same time. The idea is that what the model learns from one task can help it learn the others, a process known as inductive transfer [@caruana1997multitask]. In natural language processing (NLP), this sharing of knowledge can let a multi-task model match or even exceed the performance of separate single-task models [@chen2024mtlnlp]. The most widely used way to share knowledge is hard parameter sharing [@chen2024mtlnlp]. In this design, the tasks share most of the model, and only the last part, called a task head, is separate for each task. In a language model, the shared part is an encoder, which turns each token of a text into numbers that represent its meaning in context. Each task head then makes the predictions for its own task from these numbers [@lin2023libmtl]. Because the encoder is shared, the model reads each post only once for all its tasks and stores one encoder instead of several. @wang2021transformer gave faster prediction as one reason to use this design, although they did not measure it.

The tasks that share an encoder do not have to work on the same unit of text. The two tasks in this study work at different levels of a post. Humanitarian classification assigns the whole post one category, such as a request for supplies or damaged infrastructure [@alam2021humaid]. Named entity recognition (NER) makes a prediction for every token and marks the words that name details such as places and relief goods [@ali2026humaidner]. A post of 30 tokens therefore receives one prediction for classification and 30 for NER. Such pairings are common in NLP, and @weld2023survey reviewed many models that both identify the purpose of a sentence and find the details named by its words.

Sharing an encoder between such different tasks does not always help, however. A multi-task model can perform worse on a task than a model trained on that task alone, and this drop is called negative transfer [@mueller2022taskconflict; @elich2024paradigms]. Measuring it therefore requires a single-task model for each task, trained in the same way but on one task only. To compare such models on disaster posts, @ali2026humaidner used a different F1-score for each task. For classification, they used macro-F1, which gives every category equal weight so that rare categories count as much as common ones. For NER, they used span-level micro-F1, which counts a predicted entity as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match the label. With these scores, the change on task $t$ is the score of the multi-task model minus that of the single-task model,
$$\Delta_t = F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}$$
so a negative value shows negative transfer, and its size shows how much performance was lost. Studies of multi-task optimizers commonly summarize their results with a similar average across tasks [@liu2021cagrad; @navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo], which for two tasks is
$$\Delta_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right).$$
An average, however, can hide a loss on one task behind a gain on the other, so the change on each task is also needed to show where negative transfer occurs.

Why negative transfer occurs is less clear. Two causes are commonly described, and both concern the task gradient, which is the direction in which a task pushes the encoder to change during training [@mueller2022taskconflict]. Gradient conflict occurs when the gradients of two tasks work against each other, so a change that helps one task harms the other [@yu2020pcgrad]. Gradient dominance occurs when the gradient of one task is much larger than that of the other, so that task controls how the model changes [@chen2018gradnorm]. The link between these causes and negative transfer is not always direct, however. In multi-task language models, @mueller2022taskconflict found that differences in the sizes of the task gradients did not seem to affect negative transfer. In image models, @royer2023scalarization found that a high level of conflict usually came with a poorly performing model, but below that level the amount of conflict did not follow performance. For NER and classification in particular, @zhu2025prefinetuning found that the two tasks placed conflicting demands on how the encoder represents each token. They removed almost all of the resulting drop by adding small trainable parts for each task to the upper layers of the encoder, which changes the design of the model rather than the multi-task optimizer. The same pairing may also favor dominance, because NER gives the model a training signal for every token, while classification gives one for each post [@ali2026humaidner].

The studies reviewed here that trained a task on the whole text together with a word-level task found mixed results. In the study of @zhu2025prefinetuning, which used two small English encoders and general text, each task scored less than one point lower on average than when trained alone. Studies on disaster posts found similarly small changes, but in both directions. On Chinese typhoon posts, the shared model of @zou2025typhoon gained 0.6 points on place names and lost 0.1 points on types of damage. On English crisis posts, the shared model of @wang2021transformer scored about two points lower than single-task models on two of its three measures and three points higher on the third. Two other disaster studies measured one task only, so they could not show negative transfer on both. Khanal and Caragea [-@khanal2021location] found that location identification improved in eight of nine comparisons when trained with humanitarian classification and two other tasks, each from a different dataset, but they did not report whether classification lost performance. With fixed task weights, @ali2026humaidner found that classification performance on English disaster posts peaked in the third round of training, called an epoch, and then fell while NER was trained alongside it. They attributed this decline to dominance by NER, but they did not measure the gradients, and they compared the model with itself over time rather than with a single-task model. According to the authors, adding uncertainty weighting, a multi-task optimizer described in the next section, prevented the decline. Together, these results suggest that the effect of training the two tasks together is small and differs between datasets, so it has to be measured on the posts of interest. None of these studies used Taglish, and none compared more than two multi-task optimizers.

## Multi-Task Optimizers and Training Cost

The studies in the previous section used at most two ways of combining the tasks during training. Such a way is called a multi-task optimizer. It decides how the training signals of the tasks are combined into one update, which is a single change to the encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. The simplest optimizers add the losses of the two tasks, which measure how far the predictions of each task are from the labels, into one total loss
$$\mathcal{L} = w_1 \mathcal{L}_1 + w_2 \mathcal{L}_2,$$
where $\mathcal{L}_1$ and $\mathcal{L}_2$ are the losses of the two tasks, and $w_1$ and $w_2$ are their task weights. Equal weighting gives both weights the same value [@kurin2022unitary]. Tuned static weighting keeps the weights fixed at values chosen by trying several candidates on validation data, which is a portion of the data kept apart for choosing settings [@xin2022mtohelp]. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] called all other optimizers specialized and divided them into two families. Loss-based optimizers change the task weights during training, so their training time stays close to that of equal weighting. Gradient-based optimizers compute the gradient of each task separately and combine the gradients into one update, which needs extra computation. Peitz and Hotegni [-@peitz2025multiobjective] made a similar division. @tbl-complexity lists the 13 optimizers compared in this study, how each balances the two tasks, and its expected extra cost.

| Optimizer | Family | How It Balances the Two Tasks | Expected Extra Cost |
|:----------------------|:-----------|:----------------------------------------|:-------------|
| Equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] | Fixed | Adds the two task losses with the same weight | None |
| Tuned static weighting [@xin2022mtohelp] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with weights chosen on validation data | None during training, but extra runs to choose the weights |
| Random loss weighting [@lin2022rlw] | Loss | Draws new task weights at random at every update | None |
| Uncertainty weighting [@kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss | Gives less weight to the task the model is less certain about | None |
| FAMO [@liu2023famo] | Loss | Adjusts the weights so that both task losses fall at a balanced rate | None |
| GradNorm [@chen2018gradnorm] | Loss | Adjusts the weights so that both tasks learn at a similar speed | Small |
| MGDA [@sener2018mgda] | Gradient | Combines the task gradients into the smallest update that improves both tasks | Small |
| GradDrop [@chen2020graddrop] | Gradient | Where the task gradients point in opposite directions, keeps one direction chosen at random | Small |
| IMTL [@liu2021imtl] | Loss and gradient | Scales the task gradients so that the update favors neither task, and keeps the losses at a similar size | Small |
| PCGrad [@yu2020pcgrad] | Gradient | When the task gradients conflict, removes the part of each that works against the other | Large |
| CAGrad [@liu2021cagrad] | Gradient | Finds an update close to the average of the task gradients that most helps the task gaining least | Large |
| Nash-MTL [@navon2022bargaining] | Gradient | Treats the tasks as players that bargain over the shared update | Large |
| PCGrad with uncertainty weighting [@yu2020pcgrad; @kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss and gradient | Weights the losses as uncertainty weighting does and removes conflicts as PCGrad does | Large |

: Multi-task optimizers compared in this study and their expected extra training cost {#tbl-complexity tbl-colwidths="[24,13,45,18]"}

Note. Expected extra cost is the training time and memory that an optimizer needs beyond those of equal weighting. None means about the same as equal weighting. Small means that a separate gradient for each task is computed only at the output of the encoder. Large means that a separate gradient for each task is computed for the whole encoder, which needs at least one extra copy of the gradients, about 1.2 GB for an encoder with 300 million parameters. These are expected costs, not measurements.

The last optimizer in the table combines two others. Uncertainty weighting acts on the losses and may reduce gradient dominance, while PCGrad acts on the gradients and removes conflict. Because the two methods target the two causes of negative transfer described in the previous section, they may work better together than either does alone. @yu2020pcgrad used this combination on an image dataset with three tasks. @ali2026humaidner described uncertainty weighting, PCGrad, and GradNorm as complementary and named a direct comparison of them on disaster posts as an open direction. They chose uncertainty weighting partly because PCGrad roughly doubles memory cost, which was too high for their training setup. No earlier study reviewed here has tested this combination on text.

Whether specialized optimizers improve on simpler methods is still disputed, and several benchmarks found that they did not. @xin2022mtohelp found that, on language and image tasks, specialized optimizers did not perform better than tuned static weighting. @royer2023scalarization reached a similar result on image tasks. When extra computation was spent on searching for good fixed weights, to match the extra computation of specialized optimizers, tuned static weighting performed as well as or better than those optimizers. @kurin2022unitary added common techniques that make training more stable, such as regularization, which keeps a model from memorizing its training data. With these techniques, equal weighting performed as well as or better than the specialized optimizers, and many remaining differences were not statistically significant. The authors argued that part of the benefit of specialized optimizers comes from a similar regularizing effect. Even random weights did well. @lin2022rlw found that random loss weighting performed comparably to many specialized optimizers while running as fast as equal weighting, and they proposed it as a baseline that new optimizers should outperform.

Other studies found conditions under which specialized optimizers help. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] found that in two-task problems, particularly with similar tasks, the specialized optimizers learned weights close to equal, so equal weighting behaved much like them. Whether equal weighting matched them depended on how strongly the tasks interfered, how many tasks there were, and how much information had to be learned, and the authors concluded that specialized optimizers remain useful for complex problems. @hu2023scalarization showed in theory that, in simple linear models that are too small for their tasks, fixed task weights cannot reach some results that balance the tasks. In their experiment on robot-arm data, MGDA and a faster version of it reached such results. On text, @chai2023improving found that their gradient-based optimizer, GetMTL, outperformed equal weighting, uncertainty weighting, GradNorm, and MGDA on product review and news topic classification, although their model used a small convolutional encoder rather than a transformer, the design of modern language encoders. For NER and classification, however, PCGrad changed the average scores of the two small encoders of @zhu2025prefinetuning by only −0.1 to +0.1 points. The evidence on both sides therefore comes from images, robot tasks, molecule data, machine translation, and text classification [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform; @hu2023scalarization; @chai2023improving; @zhu2025prefinetuning]. Only Zhu et al. paired NER with classification, and they tested a single specialized optimizer. None of the studies used disaster text or a code-switched language such as Taglish.

One reason for these disagreements may be how the optimizers were compared. @xin2022mtohelp found that the results were highly sensitive to training settings and that the gains reported for specialized optimizers often disappeared when the settings of the simpler method were tuned better. When the learning rate, which sets how much the model changes at each update, was chosen from only three values, the results varied 6 to 7 times more than when only the random seed was changed. To compare optimizers fairly, Xin et al. trained every model with the same batch size, which is the number of examples used for each update, for the same number of updates, and they tuned the learning rate for each optimizer. @kurin2022unitary also chose the learning rate and the amount of regularization on validation data, and on one dataset they gave MGDA and IMTL a smaller learning rate because it gave better validation results. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] searched the learning rate and the settings that belong to each optimizer before comparing them, and argued that such a search is needed for a fair comparison. Xin et al. warned that a simpler method that is tuned less carefully can make a specialized optimizer appear better than it is.

Besides performance, the optimizers differ in training cost. This cost depends mainly on whether an optimizer computes a separate gradient for each task, and for which part of the model [@lin2023libmtl; @gama2026uniform]. Most loss-based optimizers need only one backward pass, the step that computes the gradients, as equal weighting does. Optimizers that compute a gradient for each task over the whole encoder need one backward pass for each task and must store an extra copy of the gradients. Sener and Koltun [-@sener2018mgda] lowered this cost for MGDA by computing the task gradients only at the output of the encoder, which needs a single backward pass, and other gradient-based optimizers can be run in the same way [@lin2023libmtl]. These differences give the expected costs in @tbl-complexity, and measured costs show that they can be large. Across their supervised experiments, @yu2020pcgrad reported that PCGrad took up to 12 hours to finish training against 8 hours without it, and used up to 10 GB of memory on the graphics processor against 6 GB. @xin2022mtohelp observed that computing the gradient of each task lowered training speed from about 12 to about 5 updates per second. In image models, @royer2023scalarization found that the main limit of gradient-based optimizers was their high memory use, so training them with usual batch sizes needed more processors or slower runs. @kurin2022unitary found that equal weighting had among the lowest training times, and @navon2022bargaining shortened the training time of Nash-MTL by updating its weights only once every few updates, although performance sometimes dropped. The disaster studies in the previous section reported neither training time nor memory [@ali2026humaidner; @wang2021transformer; @khanal2021location; @zou2025typhoon].

Training cost matters for disaster response for two reasons. First, a model trained on posts from earlier disasters often loses accuracy on a new event [@seeberger2022enhancing; @seeberger2025generalizing]. Keeping such a model useful may therefore require retraining it after new disasters, and every retraining run carries the full training cost again. Second, many groups that work in NLP have limited computing resources [@treviso2023efficient]. @schwartz2020green noted that the cost of computation makes deep learning research difficult for many researchers, especially those from emerging economies, and they proposed reporting computing cost alongside accuracy. Peak memory is a hard limit on such resources, because a run that needs more memory than the graphics processor has stops with an error or, with some drivers, continues at a lower speed by borrowing the main memory [@nvidia2023sysmem]. Several optimizer studies reported training time [@yu2020pcgrad; @kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @lin2022rlw; @liu2021cagrad; @navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo], but none of those reviewed here measured both training time and peak memory for a set of optimizers on a pretrained language encoder.

## Disaster Text Datasets and Taglish

Crisis informatics studies how information from social media can support disaster response, and language technologies have been part of the field from its early years [@lewis2025tapping]. The main labeled datasets for the two tasks of this study, however, are in English. HumAID contains 77,196 posts on Twitter from 19 disasters that occurred between 2016 and 2019 [@alam2021humaid]. Three crowd workers labeled each post with a humanitarian category, and only posts with agreed labels were kept. CrisisBench combined eight earlier datasets into about 141,500 posts for humanitarian classification, and its benchmark results are reported for English posts [@alam2021crisisbench]. HUMAID-NER then added entity labels to 60,000 HumAID posts, so that the same posts carry labels for both tasks [@ali2026humaidner]. It uses 10 entity types, such as CASUALTY, REQUEST, and RESOURCE, and contains about 175,000 labeled entities. Its labels follow the BIO format, which marks each token as the beginning of an entity, inside an entity, or outside any entity, so the 10 entity types give 21 possible labels for each token.

Philippine studies have used local disaster posts, but each of them trained a model for a single task. @ermino2022urgency used 4,020 posts on Twitter about Typhoon Ulysses, written in English, Tagalog, or a mix of both, to train a model that classifies posts as urgent or not urgent. An artificial neural network reached 99.17% accuracy, which is the share of posts classified correctly, on 120 validation posts. Somido and Reyes [-@somido2023actionable] classified posts on Twitter from five Philippine disasters by whether they were informative, and they noted that the slang and mixed languages in such posts make informative ones hard to find. For NER, @yute2021satellite collected 18,987 English and Tagalog posts on Twitter about the January 2020 eruption of Taal Volcano. They trained a model on 230 labeled posts to find ashfall keywords and locations, and it reached an F-score of 0.76. Other Philippine work did not train models on social media posts. @ramirez2026cultural coded comments on Facebook posts about four major typhoons from 2013 to 2021 to study how cultural values shape responses to disasters, without training a model. Local government projects applied automated analysis to incident reports rather than to posts [@yaneza2025calamba; @besario2026barangay]. None of these studies labeled the same posts for more than one task.

Only one Philippine system found in this review extracts both the type of a report and its details, and it relies on a large language model (LLM) run by a private company. Caoile and Aviles [-@caoile2025urdaneta] developed this system for the local government of Urdaneta City to collect comments from its official Facebook page during disasters. The system passes the comments through an extract, transform, and load pipeline to the GPT model of OpenAI. The model then detects the sentiment, emotion, intent, and urgency of each comment and extracts named entities such as places and barangay names. To avoid privacy and ethical concerns, the system was developed and tested on simulated comments. On these comments, the authors reported 90.2% accuracy, with similar accuracy across Filipino, Ilocano, and Taglish inputs. Unlike the model in this study, however, the system must send the comments to OpenAI for processing.

Whether an LLM can replace a model trained on labeled data differs between the two tasks. For NER, the authors of GPT-NER reported that their approach matched fully supervised models on five standard datasets and did especially well when training data was scarce [@wang2025gptner]. They also noted that access to the model was expensive, so they reported some results on a sample of only 100 test examples. For classification, smaller models trained on labeled data have still done better than LLMs that receive no training examples. @bucher2024finetuned found this in every classification task they tested. On the crisis posts of CrisisBench, the best LLM tested by @mcdaniel2024zeroshot reached a weighted F1-score of 0.828 against 0.883 for a trained RoBERTa model.

Language is a further obstacle for any such model, because Philippine posts often mix more than one language. Code-switching is the practice of alternating between two or more languages in continuous conversation [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. Taglish, which mixes Tagalog and English, has been argued to be the everyday common language of the Philippines, and Filipino text collected from social media typically contains some code-switching [@montalan2025batayan]. Filipino, however, lacks many of the datasets, tools, and pretrained models available for English [@cruz2022tagalog], and code-switched text is itself a setting with few resources [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. Tagalog NER datasets exist, but they come from news reports, internet pages, and historical newspapers rather than from disaster posts [@miranda2023tlunifiedner; @ramos2023tfnerd; @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. Because the language and the available resources differ, findings from English disaster posts may not carry over to Taglish. This applies to multi-task optimizers in particular, since Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] found that whether they help depends on the problem, such as how strongly the tasks interfere.

A model for Taglish therefore needs an encoder pretrained on both Filipino and English. SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, developed by AI Singapore, was pretrained on 13 languages, including Filipino and English [@aisingapore2026sealion]. It follows the ModernBERT design, which was built to be fast and efficient in memory [@warner2025modernbert]. Filipino, however, makes up only about 2.5% of its pretraining data, compared with about 35% for English [@aisingapore2026sealion]. The closest earlier study, which labeled the same posts for both tasks, used RoBERTa-large, an English encoder [@ali2026humaidner]. Because Filipino is a small share of the pretraining data and the earlier study used a different encoder, how well this encoder performs on each task with Taglish posts has to be measured directly.

A new dataset for these tasks also has to show that its labels can be trusted. Inter-annotator agreement measures how often annotators who label the same items independently give the same labels. Cohen's kappa measures this agreement between two annotators on category labels and corrects for the agreement expected by chance [@cohen1960coefficient]. Landis and Koch [-@landis1977measurement] described kappa values from 0.61 to 0.80 as substantial agreement and values above 0.80 as almost perfect. Earlier disaster and Tagalog datasets reported such measures. HumAID reported agreement among its crowd workers with Fleiss' kappa and other measures [@alam2021humaid]. For NER, however, the value of kappa depends on which tokens are counted. On Tagalog NER, @miranda2023tlunifiedner reported a kappa of 0.81 over all tokens but 0.65 over annotated tokens only, and @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner reported 0.86 and 0.72 on historical Tagalog text. Both also reported an F1-score between annotators, of 0.91 and 0.74, which avoids this choice by comparing whole entities. Not every dataset measured agreement. TF-NERD, a Tagalog dataset with 12 entity types, was labeled by one annotator, and its authors listed the lack of an agreement measure as a limitation [@ramos2023tfnerd].

No dataset found in this review labels the same Taglish posts for both humanitarian classification and NER. The Philippine datasets each carry labels for one task, and the only dataset found with labels for both of these tasks, HUMAID-NER, is in English. The closest dataset in another language, that of @zou2025typhoon, labels Chinese posts for types of damage and place names. Without such a dataset, single-task and multi-task models cannot be compared on the same Taglish posts, so negative transfer between these tasks cannot be measured.

: Algorithmic Literature Taxonomy Matrix {#tbl-matrix tbl-colwidths="[14,22,21,19,24]"}

Taken together, the rows show where earlier work stops short of this study. The disaster studies used English or Chinese posts, the Philippine studies trained a model for one task or relied on an LLM run by a private company, and the optimizer studies used mostly images, robot tasks, and molecules. Only @zhu2025prefinetuning paired NER with classification, on English text outside disasters and with one specialized optimizer. Training time was reported mainly by the optimizer studies, and memory by only two of them. No row combines Taglish text, both tasks, several multi-task optimizers, and measured training cost.

## Synthesis of Related Literature and Studies

The reviewed studies show three trends. First, multi-task models for disaster posts have been trained on English or Chinese text [@ali2026humaidner; @wang2021transformer; @khanal2021location; @zou2025typhoon], while Philippine disaster studies trained models for one task [@ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @yute2021satellite] or sent the text to an LLM run by a private company [@caoile2025urdaneta]. Second, training a task on the whole text together with a word-level task has given small and mixed changes in performance. Some tasks lost a little, others gained, and in one study classification declined during training [@zhu2025prefinetuning; @zou2025typhoon; @wang2021transformer; @khanal2021location; @ali2026humaidner]. Third, many multi-task optimizers exist, but they were tested mainly on images, robot tasks, and molecules, and studies disagree on whether they improve on fixed task weights [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @royer2023scalarization; @hu2023scalarization; @gama2026uniform; @chai2023improving].

These trends leave four gaps, one for each research question. The first gap concerns single-task performance on Taglish posts. No dataset found in this review labels the same Taglish posts for both tasks, and results from English posts cannot simply be carried over, because Filipino makes up only a small share of the pretraining data of SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M [@aisingapore2026sealion]. The first research question therefore measures single-task performance on a new Taglish dataset, whose agreement between annotators is measured as in earlier datasets [@alam2021humaid; @miranda2023tlunifiedner]. The second gap concerns the design of a model for both tasks. The disaster models that paired classification with a word-level task used English or Chinese encoders [@ali2026humaidner; @khanal2021location; @zou2025typhoon], and the Philippine system that handles both sends the text to OpenAI [@caoile2025urdaneta]. The second research question designs such a model for Taglish with SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, using the hard parameter sharing of the closest earlier study [@ali2026humaidner].

The third gap concerns the choice of multi-task optimizer. None of the disaster studies compared more than two optimizers, and evidence from other fields does not settle the choice. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] found that specialized optimizers behaved like equal weighting mainly when the two tasks were similar, for example when their task heads and labels were alike. The two tasks in this study differ in both, because NER makes a prediction for every token while classification makes one for each post, so specialized optimizers may behave differently from equal weighting for this pairing. Training cost has also been left out. No study reviewed here measured both training time and peak memory for a set of optimizers on a pretrained language encoder, and none of the disaster studies reported either. @xin2022mtohelp asked whether the extra computation of specialized optimizers could be spent more effectively, but no study reviewed here weighed training cost against negative transfer for these tasks. The third research question therefore compares the 13 optimizers on both and selects the one that the final model uses.

The fourth gap concerns the value of one multi-task model over two single-task models. A multi-task model stores one encoder instead of two, and @wang2021transformer and @ali2026humaidner argued that it is cheaper to run than two separate models. None of the disaster studies, however, measured the storage or processing time of a multi-task model against single-task models, and whether these savings come with lower predictive performance on Taglish posts is unknown. The fourth research question compares the final model with the single-task models in predictive performance, training time, peak memory, storage, and processing time.

Together, the four research questions bridge these gaps in order. The study builds a Taglish dataset labeled for both tasks, sets single-task baselines on it, and designs a multi-task model with an encoder pretrained on Filipino. It then trains 13 candidate models that differ only in their optimizer. They share the same encoder, data, and laptop, and the learning rate of each is chosen in the same way, as the benchmarks reviewed here did, so that differences in negative transfer and training cost can be traced to the optimizer [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Because the literature disagrees on whether specialized optimizers improve on fixed task weights, equal weighting serves as the reference, and another optimizer is chosen only if it reduces negative transfer significantly without lowering the score on either task. Finally, comparing the final model with the single-task models shows what one model for both tasks gains or loses against two separate models, in predictive performance and in cost, on Taglish typhoon posts. Chapter 3 describes how the study answers these questions.
